common_name: Crimson King Camellia (Large Single Red Fragrant Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Crimson King grows quickly into an open, upright screen and takes more direct sun than most sasanquas without scorching.

directions: Crimson King produces large single flowers, up to 5 inches across, in a glowing crimson-red with twisted, slightly ruffled petals set off by a prominent boss of golden stamens; the blooms carry a light fragrance uncommon among sasanquas. Growth is notably fast and open, forming an upright to spreading large shrub or small tree that works well as an informal screen, background planting, or trained espalier where its vigor can be put to use. Unlike many sasanqua selections bred for a compact habit, Crimson King needs room to develop and benefits from occasional thinning cuts right after flowering to keep the framework from becoming leggy. Provide consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil and mulch to protect its shallow root system through summer heat.

common_name: Paradise Belinda Camellia (Large Single Pink Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Paradise Belinda, bred by Bob Cherry of Paradise Plants in Australia, flowers over an exceptionally long autumn-through-winter season.

directions: Paradise Belinda carries large single flowers, to roughly 4 inches across, in a glowing clear pink with a bright cluster of golden stamens at the center, opening over one of the longest bloom windows of any sasanqua selection. Its dense, well-branched habit stays reasonably tidy without heavy pruning, making it useful for hedging, screening, or as a specimen where extended fall-to-winter color is wanted. As part of the Australian-bred Paradise series, it was selected specifically for vigor and floriferousness compared to older sasanqua cultivars. Grow in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune lightly after the last flowers fade if size control is needed.

common_name: Star Above Star Camellia (Semi-Double Shell-Pink and White Star-Petaled Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and strong wind; Star Above Star won the Ralph Peer Sasanqua Seedling Award in 1969.

directions: Star Above Star bears showy semi-double flowers of white overlaid with shell-pink shading, with pointed petals arranged so one star-shaped whorl appears layered on top of another, centered on bright yellow stamens. The vigorous, upright, bushy habit makes it a good candidate for hedging, screening, or a specimen feature where its late-fall-to-early-spring flowering can be appreciated up close. It is more sun-tolerant than Camellia japonica but still colors and flowers best with some protection from intense afternoon exposure and wind, which can bruise the ruffled petals. Keep soil evenly moist and acidic, and prune only lightly right after bloom since next season's buds set on the current year's growth.

common_name: Jennifer Susan Camellia (Soft Pink Curled-Petal Compact Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Jennifer Susan arose as a chance seedling in New South Wales, Australia, first flowering in 1959, and stays compact enough for low hedges or pots.

directions: Jennifer Susan produces abundant soft rosy-pink, semi-double to informal-double flowers with distinctively curled petals surrounding a bright golden center, opening from autumn into early winter on a compact, tidy, well-branched shrub. Its dense habit and moderate mature size make it better suited than many larger sasanquas to low hedging, foundation plantings, and container culture on a shaded patio. Once established it tolerates light frost and short dry spells better than younger plants, though consistent moisture during establishment improves flowering. Grow in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil with a protective mulch layer, and shape lightly right after bloom if needed.

common_name: Valley Fire Pieris (Fiery Red New-Growth Cold-Hardy Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Valley Fire is noted for unusually good cold hardiness and disease resistance compared to older Pieris japonica selections.

directions: Valley Fire opens bright pink flower buds in late winter to early spring, unfurling into cascading clusters of fragrant, bell-shaped white flowers against foliage that emerges a vivid fiery red and gradually matures to deep green as the season progresses. It grows into a larger, more vigorous shrub than many compact Pieris cultivars, making it useful as a specimen, informal screen, or backdrop for smaller shade plantings. Selected in part for improved resistance to lace bug and winter dieback, it holds up better than older cultivars in colder or more exposed sites. Provide moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil, shelter from harsh winter wind and afternoon sun, and prune lightly after flowering only if needed to control size.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Carnaval holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its combination of variegated foliage and reliable spring bloom.

directions: Carnaval is grown chiefly for its small, dark green leaves edged in creamy white, with new spring growth emerging bright red flushed pink before settling into the mature variegated pattern, giving the shrub multi-season color even without flowers. Creamy-white buds set the previous autumn open in early spring into sprays of small, clear white, urn-shaped flowers typical of the species. Its upright, moderately compact habit suits foundation plantings, woodland borders, or mixed shade beds where the variegated foliage can brighten a dim corner year-round. Grow in consistently moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil, shelter young plants from harsh winter sun and wind, and avoid heavy pruning, which removes the colorful new growth.
